passage: Last week I had a cold, and my voice came out nasal and rough. When I answered in class, Nandini copied me in a silly voice and some kids laughed. My face went hot. I wanted to say, “It's my cold!” but nothing came. That evening Mummy gave me warm water and said the voice was because my nose was blocked and my throat was sore. It was my body, not my mood. Next day I told Nandini, “I'm not sad or grumpy, I'm just sick.” She looked ashamed and said sorry. I'm Farida, and I understand my voice a bit better now.

qa.q: What did Nandini do when Farida answered in class?
qa.a: She copied Farida in a silly voice.

qa.q: How did Farida feel when the class laughed, and how do you know?
qa.a: Farida felt embarrassed, since Farida's face went hot and words to explain would not come.

qa.q: What did Farida do that helped clear things up?
qa.a: Farida told Nandini it was a cold, not sadness or grumpiness, which explained the voice.

qa.q: Why might Nandini have misread Farida's voice?
qa.a: Nandini may have thought the strange voice meant a mood or was just funny, without thinking it came from a cold.

grounding: A nasal, raspy voice reflects a cold and body state, not mood, and mocking it is a misreading.

passage: Counsellor's note, Class 5. Dilnaz came to see me because some classmates called her voice “angry crow.” Her voice has been raspy for four days after cheering at the sports day. She wondered aloud if she sounded mean. I explained that a raspy voice usually tells us something about the throat, not the feelings, and that a doctor could look if it keeps going or worries her. With her permission, I spoke to Maria, who had joined in the teasing. Maria said she had assumed Dilnaz was grumpy. She agreed to apologise. Dilnaz drank water and left smiling a little. Ms. Maria's class will hear a short talk on voices. Counsellor.

qa.q: How long has Dilnaz's voice been raspy?
qa.a: Four days.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz worried about when she came to the counsellor?
qa.a: She wondered whether her raspy voice made her sound mean to others.

qa.q: What could Dilnaz do if the raspy voice keeps going?
qa.a: She could tell a trusted adult and check with the doctor if it keeps going or worries her.

qa.q: Why might Maria have joined in the teasing?
qa.a: Maria assumed Dilnaz was grumpy because of how she sounded, so she read a body state as a mood.

grounding: A raspy voice from shouting reflects body state, peers misread it as mood, and an adult teaches that voice quality is body first.

passage: Monday. Aditi's diary. My voice is a frog today. I screamed so much at Saturday's kabaddi final that now I can only croak. In class, when Deepika asked to borrow my compass, I said, “Take it,” and it came out rough and low. She pulled her hand back. “Why are you angry with me?” I wasn't! I tried to explain, and it came out even more like a growl, and she looked hurt. So I wrote in my rough book: NOT ANGRY. LOST MY VOICE SHOUTING FOR OUR TEAM. She read it and burst out laughing. Ma'am let me write my answers today. I'm drinking warm water with honey.

qa.q: What made Aditi lose the voice?
qa.a: Aditi screamed a lot at Saturday's kabaddi final.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she pulled her hand back?
qa.a: Deepika felt hurt and worried, reading Aditi's rough, low voice as anger at her.

qa.q: What did Aditi do to fix the misunderstanding?
qa.a: Aditi wrote a clear note explaining the voice was lost from shouting, not anger.

qa.q: What would change if Aditi had just stayed silent?
qa.a: Deepika might have gone on believing Aditi was angry with her, and felt hurt all day.

grounding: Shows a raspy voice from shouting being misread as anger, when voice quality reflects body state first.

passage: Chinmay had a heavy cold, and when Deepika Teacher asked him to read the poem aloud in the village school, it came out thick and nasal: “The bango tree by our dore.” Three boys at the back honked like geese. Chinmay's ears went red, and he stopped. Deepika Teacher put down her chalk. “His nose is blocked. That's all a voice like that means: a cold, not a joke. Mine sounded the same last week.” She poured Chinmay a cup of warm water from her flask. “Read again when you're ready.” He finished the poem. The boys stayed quiet.

qa.q: What did Deepika Teacher give Chinmay?
qa.a: She poured him a cup of warm water from her flask.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling when the boys honked?
qa.a: Chinmay felt embarrassed and hurt, his ears going red, so he stopped reading.

qa.q: How did Deepika Teacher handle the mocking?
qa.a: She stopped the lesson, explained that a nasal voice means a cold, shared that hers sounded the same, and let Chinmay continue when ready.

qa.q: How did the boys at the back read Chinmay's voice?
qa.a: They treated the nasal voice as something funny to mock, not realising it simply came from a blocked nose.

grounding: Shows peers mocking a child's nasal voice from a cold, and a teacher explaining that voice quality is body state first.

passage: Every spring in Hanoi, Tuan's voice went scratchy and rough, like sandpaper. Aiko, who had only moved there in January, didn't know that. When she asked if he wanted to be partners for the science poster, he croaked, “Sure, fine,” and coughed. Aiko's face fell. He sounds so grumpy. Maybe he doesn't want to work with me. She almost asked someone else. Then she noticed his red, watery eyes and the tissues piled on his desk. “Are you sick?” “Allergies,” he rasped. “The flowers outside. I'm happy to be partners, I promise. My voice just sounds cross.” Aiko laughed and pushed the window shut.

qa.q: When does Tuan's voice go scratchy?
qa.a: Every spring in Hanoi, Tuan's voice goes scratchy and rough.

qa.q: What was Aiko feeling when Tuan croaked his answer?
qa.a: Aiko felt disappointed and worried that Tuan didn't want to work with her, reading the rough voice as grumpiness.

qa.q: What clues helped Aiko read the voice correctly?
qa.a: Tuan's red, watery eyes and the pile of tissues showed he was unwell, so she asked instead of assuming.

qa.q: How does Tuan feel about his spring voice?
qa.a: Tuan knows his voice sounds cross during allergy season, which is why he promised Aiko he was happy to be partners.

grounding: Shows a raspy voice from allergies being misread as grumpiness, when it reflects body state, not mood.

passage:
On Monday, Uma answered roll call in a voice like sandpaper. "Present."

Three boys at the back cracked up. "Uma's turned into a frog!" "Or she's in a mood. Listen to her, all growly."

Uma's cheeks went pink. She croaked, "I'm not in a mood," which made it worse.

Nazia Ma'am put down the register. "Who was at the inter-school sports meet on Saturday?" Half the class raised hands. "And who was screaming for our relay team the loudest?" Everybody pointed at Uma. "So that voice is her body telling us about Saturday, not a mood. Throats get tired, like legs. Colds and allergies do the same. Uma, sip some water and rest it today."

qa.q: What did the boys say Uma had turned into?
qa.a: A frog.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when the boys laughed at her voice?
qa.a: Embarrassed and a bit frustrated, as her pink cheeks show, especially when her croaky denial made it worse.

qa.q: How did Nazia Ma'am correct the misreading?
qa.a: She reminded the class that Uma had screamed for the relay team on Saturday and explained that a voice reflects the body first, like tired legs, not a mood.

qa.q: How did the boys read Uma's raspy voice?
qa.a: They took it as a joke and as a grumpy mood, missing that her throat was simply tired from cheering.

grounding: It shows peers mocking a child's raspy voice as a mood, and a teacher explaining that voice quality reflects the body first.
